strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: accelerating Diffusion Policy inference for real-time robotic control
Comprehensive empirical characterization of temporal similarity patterns across network blocks with insightful visualizations (Figures 1, 10, 11)
Extensive experimental validation across multiple real-world robotic benchmarks and simulation tasks with thorough ablation studies
Good reproducibility: detailed algorithm descriptions, extensive supplementary tables, and commitment to open-source release
Solid analysis of error propagation mechanisms in FFN blocks (Section 3.3) that provides useful insights for caching design
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: straightforward application of dynamic programming to feature similarity-based scheduling; selective computation caching and cosine similarity are established techniques
Weak theoretical justification: the critical assumption that maximizing global feature similarity preserves task performance is never rigorously justified or validated
Proposition 3.1 provides only first-order Taylor approximation without error bounds; no theoretical guarantees on when the method preserves performance
Bubbling Union Algorithm appears ad-hoc: post-hoc observation (Section 3.3) rather than principled design; simple heuristic without theoretical motivation for its specific two-stage approach

Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing comparisons with other DP acceleration methods (distillation, pruning); TeaCache designed for VLM generation, not DP; DDIM is algorithmic alternative, not fair acceleration baseline
Moderate speedup gains: 3× is valuable but not transformative; several tasks show 20%+ performance degradation (Table 1: Transport/Kitchen with S=5)
Narrow evaluation scope: only Diffusion Policy tested; only robotic manipulation domain; no generalization analysis for different model sizes/architectures
Hyperparameter sensitivity not addressed: number of cache update steps S appears task-dependent; no principled guidance for setting S, n in practice

Ablation results contradict main motivation: Block-wise ACS underperforms Unified ACS (Fig. 7b), suggesting inter-block coordination dominates rather than block-specific adaptation justifying the complexity

strengths: Well-motivated core insight: Non-uniform temporal feature similarity patterns across transformer blocks is compelling and well-demonstrated (Figure 1), providing clear justification for block-wise rather than uniform caching

Solid theoretical framework: Clear problem formulation via dynamic programming (Eqs. 5-9), rigorous error propagation analysis (Section 3.3, Proposition 3.1), and theoretical justification for both ACS and BUA components

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive benchmarks including real-world Franka robot tasks and multiple simulation environments with detailed metrics, thorough ablation studies (Figure 7) clearly demonstrating contribution of each component, and multiple similarity metrics tested

Practical effectiveness and deployability: Achieves 3× inference speedup with minimal performance degradation in a training-free, plugin-compatible format, making it immediately applicable to existing systems without retraining

Strong reproducibility: Detailed algorithmic descriptions, complete hyperparameter documentation, use of public datasets, extensive supplementary visualizations, and promised code release enable easy reproduction

Clear presentation: Generally well-written paper with intuitive figures (especially Figure 3's framework diagram), appropriate mathematical notation, and good organization across main paper and appendices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Cache-based acceleration and dynamic programming scheduling are well-established techniques; the Bubbling Union Algorithm is straightforward (essentially top-k selection with recursive updates); contribution is primarily engineering/application-oriented rather than methodological innovation

Experimental scope limitations: Real-world evaluation restricted to single Franka robot configuration with unknown generalization to other morphologies; simulation tasks are relatively simple manipulation primitives; success rates sometimes modest (52-63% for challenging tasks); some baselines could be stronger (no comparison with learnable caching or attention-based scheduling)

Insufficient hyperparameter analysis: Multiple hyperparameters introduced (S, n, β) with limited sensitivity analysis; Section A.7 only examines π parameter; broader ablation and interaction effects between ACS and BUA not thoroughly explored; unclear guidelines for setting parameters on new tasks

Theoretical gaps and assumptions: Assumption A.1 (twice continuously differentiable activation with bounded second derivative) is strong and may not hold for ReLU-based networks; error propagation model in Section 3.3 is simplified; missing analysis of worst-case scenarios and failure modes

Missing important analyses: No computational overhead quantification for DP solver despite claims of 'virtually no cost'; no memory footprint analysis; absence of statistical significance testing despite high variance in results (e.g., Transport task); limited discussion of scalability to larger models or more complex tasks

Incomplete experimental comparisons: Some baselines appear suboptimal (Uniform caching not fine-tuned for problem); no comparison with recent efficient inference methods (token pruning, adaptive computation); DP-T baseline choice insufficiently justified

Presentation issues: Dense supplementary material with some hard-to-read heatmaps (Figures 10-32) that could benefit from better resolution; some notation could be clearer (e.g., φ in Eq. 4); paper length could be reduced by reorganizing content
